1	\section{Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:conclusion}
3	
4	We tested whether unpaired taxonomy-guided error injection---effective for tool-use agents---transfers to embodied planning. On ALFWorld, TaxEI provides no statistically significant improvement over clean training ($-8.6$pp, $p{=}0.054$). Two competing hypotheses explain this: embodied planning may lack the discrete, observable error structure required for injection to help, or the absence of recovery pairing (present in PALADIN) may render standalone errors unlearnable. We additionally identify a dose-dependent dual regime (3-seed confirmed at 25\%/50\%): deterministic degradation at moderate injection, chaotic seed-dependent outcomes at high injection. We also observe a per-operator local/global split (exploratory, $N{=}11$--$12$).
5	
6	Based on our results and the two competing hypotheses, we suggest that practitioners considering error injection for embodied tasks check four properties: (1)~are errors discrete and observable? (2)~can recovery be achieved locally? (3)~does the task provide immediate feedback? (4)~are errors paired with explicit recovery demonstrations? These criteria require validation in other environments.
7	
8	Future work should first test recovery-paired injection on ALFWorld to disentangle the task-structure hypothesis from recovery-pairing effects, then replicate on a second environment (e.g., WebShop) and investigate the seed-initialization $\times$ injection interaction observed at high doses.

tool_args.old_string:
\paragraph{Limitations.}
We evaluate on a single environment (ALFWorld, 47 tasks) with one base model. Three seeds provide limited statistical power; the 10\% dose-response uses a single seed (25\%/50\% confirmed across 3 seeds). TaxEI/Random use $2.1\times$ more training data than Vanilla; the fixed-size ablation controls for this. Per-operator analysis ($N{=}11$--$12$) is exploratory. ALFWorld uses a text-based interface where errors produce discrete feedback (``Nothing happens''), partially resembling tool-use error observability. Vision-based embodied tasks with continuous state spaces may exhibit different error injection dynamics. We compare only error injection variants; other augmentation strategies (e.g., paraphrasing, trajectory diversification) were not tested, leaving open whether the negative result generalizes to all off-distribution augmentation at this data scale.
tool_args.new_string: We additionally observe a training-evaluation paradox at $\geq$25\% injection, where models achieve lower training loss but worse evaluation performance (Appendix~\ref{app:paradox}).

tool_args.old_string: We hypothesize that the transfer failure stems from structural differences between tool-use and embodied planning (Table~\ref{tab:structural} in Appendix). In tool-use, errors produce discrete signals (API error codes) mapping to specific recovery actions; taxonomy labels encode this mapping. In embodied planning, errors propagate silently---picking the wrong object produces no error message, and recovery requires replanning from an unknown state.
tool_args.new_string: We hypothesize that the transfer failure stems from structural differences between tool-use and embodied planning. Table~\ref{tab:structural} (Appendix) identifies five dimensions where these domains diverge: error signal (discrete API codes vs.\ diffuse wrong-object errors), observability (explicit stack traces vs.\ silent failures), recovery scope (local retry vs.\ global replanning), feedback timing (immediate vs.\ delayed), and error locality (single-step vs.\ cascading). In tool-use, taxonomy labels encode a direct mapping from error type to recovery action. In embodied planning, errors propagate silently---picking the wrong object produces no error message, and recovery requires replanning from an unknown state.

tool_args.old_string:
The uniform 0\% detection rate (\S\ref{sec:recovery}) may reflect that SFT does not internalize taxonomy labels when they appear only as prompt prefixes---the training objective (next-token prediction) does not incentivize error classification, so models learn trajectory patterns rather than error type distinctions.

We additionally observe a training-evaluation paradox at $\geq$25\% injection, where models achieve lower training loss but worse evaluation performance (Appendix~\ref{app:paradox}).
tool_args.new_string: The uniform 0\% detection rate (\S\ref{sec:recovery}) may reflect that SFT does not internalize taxonomy labels when they appear only as prompt prefixes---the training objective (next-token prediction) does not incentivize error classification, so models learn trajectory patterns rather than error type distinctions. This suggests a fundamental limitation of direct SFT mixing for error-awareness: without an explicit classification or contrastive objective, taxonomy labels serve as surface tokens that do not transfer to inference-time error recognition. Methods that use preference optimization \cite{song2024eto} may better incentivize error discrimination.
